text: Static typing in doeff. A type checker follows your effects out to the handler, and back.
It checks three things. First, the value each effect answers with.
Second, the effects a program may yield.
And third, the value a handler answers with.
An effect declares its answer type. ReadClock is an EffectBase of int: its handler answers with an int.
A generic parent works too, and the same type can be read at run time: WriteShared answers a bool.
An effect on plain EffectBase leaves its answer type unknown: Any.
Yield from an effect: the program pauses, the effect travels out, and a handler sends back the answer.
The checker knows that answer's type. now is an int, in pyright and in mypy.
A bare yield runs exactly the same way, but the checker only sees Any.
Yield from a sub-program gives its result type: spent is an int.
The at-do decorator keeps three things of the function it wraps: its parameters, its effects, and its result.
The parameters. Calling elapsed with a string is a type error.
The effects. Yielding an effect outside the declared set is a type error too.
And the result. Running the program under its handler gives an int.
A handler answers an effect by resuming k, the rest of the program, with a value.
typed resume checks that value against the effect's answer type. One thousand is an int, so elapsed returns six hundred.
Answering ReadClock with a string is refused by the checker.
A handler that no effect can reach is refused twice: by the checker, and by the handler decorator when it runs.
The same types can be read at run time, so tools that cannot run pyright, such as the Hy checker, read one source of truth.
What is not typed: Ask and Get answer Any, because the environment and the state are dynamic.
And whether the handlers cover a program's effects is not a type error. Without the clock handler, run raises UnhandledEffect.
In doeff, effects carry their types. The checker follows them out to the handler, and back.
